They didn't turn out like these fellas turn out the day, but they all decorate umbrellas. You know how it cost them 15, 12 dollars to decorate one of them umbrellas? I'm telling you. Fans, they…

265.t: Dispute over marshals at Sunday's parade; Slow Drag and Pork Chop
265.s: The club disliked marching behind the hired band's marshals; Wilson knows Slow Drag and Pork Chop, and a dancer named Rankin.
265.q: Well he wanted this fella see. But see we should, see my marshal should have led the band, then my second marshal should have led the club. So that's the way we turned out. I have a number one marshal, he leads the procession. And my second grand marshal, he leads the members, the banner. But as he…

265.t: Showing the decorated fan and badge
265.s: Wilson shows his decorated fan and officer badge, who makes them, and the colors.
265.q: This is the fan. No, they don't be all made like this. That's decorated. All of them have fans similar to that, but different style of fans, but they have different decorations.

138.t: Carnival parade contracts and Nick's brief time
138.s: Laine says he played all the carnival parades and balls under Braun and Moss contracts, and La Rocca played with him but not much.
138.ch: Photo session: wagons, parades and goodbyes
138.q: Yeah. When Captain Braun had the contract for years and years, played. Then... Benny Moss. Benny Moss. Benny Moss got it. Yeah. I played. And some other fella got it. Nice-hazard guy got it.

138.t: Five jobs in one Mardi Gras day
138.s: Laine describes playing five engagements in a single Mardi Gras day, from advertising for a doctor to parades and a ball, while a visitor departs.
138.q: Yes, several times he came here. He came here a few times, see. So, music was a wonderful thing one time ago. Oh, boy, day and night I'd be going. Now, there's a coincidence. If you were to tell a man he played five tours, five jobs, five engagements in one day, he'd laugh at you. He'd laugh at…

138.t: Kindergarten band in Biloxi and the lost spirit of Mardi Gras bands
138.s: Around 1910 Laine's band of kids in Biloxi plays Kentucky Days and wins over a soldier band; he then says ragtime bands beat stiff military bands in parades and he ran up to five bands.

628.t: Mardi Gras and carnival club parades
628.s: He played the white carnival parades for the Eleonora and Lions clubs, for about four years with the Lions and three with another marching club.
628.ch: Police work, brass bands and carnival
628.q: the carnival? Oh yeah, I worked those white parades. I worked the carnival club, I worked the Eleonora, the Eleonora club, worked for the Lions, and jumped you know from one year to the other because they all paid big prices you know. I worked for the Lions for about four years straight. When I was…

628.t: Committee work and Carnival Eve parade
628.s: Williams says he is on a committee for a club and tells of a parade he played on Carnival Eve.
628.q: Yeah. I played one on Carnival Eve. They parade around on Carnival Eve? Carnival Eve, yeah. That's the scene of the mayor from Pumetum that day. And they would like to have got it that Sunday, but there was too much other activity and there wouldn't be enough protection for them. So by being the…

628.t: Corner Club and carnival club marches
628.s: They discuss playing for the Corner Club, the early start times and long walks of the Buzzers and Lions, and which parade is the easiest job.
628.q: Corner Club uptown. Mm-hmm. On Washington Avenue. Same place I guess they all know. They used to be around on that street growing up. They wasn't out where they at. Mm-hmm.

632.t: Fancy drill by social club marching units
632.s: The Olympians' paramilitary unit and Odd Fellows' men's and ladies' drill teams in his photographs, and how drill teams get confused.
632.q: Not from the musicians particularly. No, no, I mean the- Oh, the marching groups? The, uh, the social organizations. Oh, yeah. There were, uh, in fact some of the photographs show, in particular show, and as I remember this was a young men's Olympians organization, I think. Yeah. That had both,…

632.t: Parade stops at bars and homes; sandwiches in the umbrella
632.s: Parades stopped at bars and homes while bands played outside; the interviewer recalls Herman Sherman teaching him to hide sandwiches in an umbrella.
632.q: Obviously, obviously you can't roll your brawly very tightly if you're carrying sandwiches. No, it was very loose, in fact.

632.t: Stumbling on a brass band parade near General Ogden Street
632.s: In 1951 Steinau heard a parade near his apartment; Allen talks about parades around town and how he learned of them.
632.q: But, you know, it was possible. In fact, not only possible, I think maybe even inevitable, if you happen to start noticing things like that, that you ran into things. I had a, in, I guess it must have been sometime in the fall of 1951, I had a small apartment on General Ogden Street. And one Sunday…

128.s: Society parades once walked slowly and strictly, with members and police keeping the crowd back from the band.
128.q: oh yeah I wake up most of my wife was a brass band when I was young but played plenty parades nothing let me try my pit for any periods well I was young then running my twenties now man who is I could play them not for one but I think we did that walk in population see every year ago we used to…

128.t: Labor Day parades and all-night fairground dances
128.s: Societies' bands met at Elk's Place, paraded all day, then played at the fairground until morning.

128.t: First brass band parade and pay
128.s: Robinson recalls his first street parade on carnival day, the pay, and walking the route.
128.q: The first brass band I played with. See the New Orleans? That was on the carnival day, Budapetit. Budapetit on the carnival day. And that was the first parade I played too. Budapetit. With old man Parker, Willie Parker.

292.t: Zulu and Rex arriving by boat, carnival in Algiers
292.s: Memories of Rex and Zulu arriving by river, taking her daughter Effie to watch, and the Algiers parade.
292.q: I went for coffee and donuts, but not when I was young. No, later on I did. When I pass that now, I wish I could go in there and get coffee and donuts, but I just don't go.

292.s: Carnival then was much like now but with more masks; where she watched parades; whether people drank and fought more.
292.q: I think carnival was the same as it is today. Pretty much the same. Yeah, only we had more masks, more people masks than they do now.

292.t: Carnival marching clubs and jazz funerals
292.s: Marching clubs, women's night parades, social clubs with colored bands, jazz funeral music, and band sizes from 1917 to 1930.
292.q: The garden? They have some clubs, women, but it would be too expensive for me to join. There's a lot of these night parades of women. Venus is all women and quite a few others. But it's a lot of expensive long times.

644.t: Fake parade bands and the fight with the union boss
644.s: Lala explains how he padded parade bands with non-playing men in uniforms, with Emile Gonzales on drums, until Benny Morris made him stop.
644.q: I used to have fights, advertised fights. But only six men in a way, six men, you know? In Italian, in the foiniture wagon, it's an old-time foiniture wagon. Hell, when I got two, I had a 60-man there playing the parade, all, just to go and see the fight. I was playing the marailles, I didn't care.…

644.t: The 1919 streetcar strike parade and the broken cornet
644.s: Lala tells how he played behind strike speakers with Schilling in 1919, walked back, smashed his cornet on a post and had to borrow Joe Hall's for work.
644.q: They had circles that week. I'm going to tell you, the last parade I've prayed in my life. The last time I prayed. It was in 1919, they had a car strike. See? And we had to walk from the heritage, we were all human, you see? But we had to hide outside men. So, Shilling got a job. Around 1919. 18 or…

644.t: Italian bands, picnics and the St. Rosalie parade
644.s: Lala recalls playing with Italian bands at picnics, Professor Costa, the St. Rosalie parade, and relatives who played.
644.ch: Laine, ragtime bands and the union
644.q: Oh, the same Uncle? Yeah. Angry, yeah. You get that, yeah? Because we're the boys from the old England. Yeah, that's right. They said they stole that song. They said they stole that song. They said they stole that song.

849.t: Parade from the cutoff to Algiers through open fields
849.s: He recalls a Labor Day parade walked from the cutoff to Algiers, played to cows and horses.
849.q: And you know, do you know this? You're playing your horn, walking on the road like that. Do you know your inside be dry as anything? Look like you make your throat be dry. Now that happened to us one time. From the cutoff. You ever been going down to the cutoff? Down on the other side. Yeah. We…

849.t: Second lines, traffic and police over parades
849.s: He discusses parade permits, traffic and streetcar routes, and monthly gatherings of old musicians.
849.q: They ain't going to have it. They wouldn't give them no punishment. I wonder. Well, they overdo the thing. You understand what I mean? They block up all them buses. And that second line, they take us all over. You understand what I mean? They can have a parade like they're supposed to have it. No,…

849.t: Playing parades: heat, rough streets and reading music
849.s: He talks about parades with John Casimir, the heat, stone streets, and playing hymns without reading the music.
849.q: Play with John. I play with, what you call, this boy, George Williams. You know. Well, I tell you the truth, I'm going to be straight and tell you about them parades. That sun's been a little too hot, man. That didn't use me walking all that hot sun like that. It's hot in that sun, man.

58.t: Walking in parades and carrying a Mardi Gras parade alone
58.s: Punch says fingering made him misstep with the drum and tells of playing a whole parade when the other trumpeter failed to show.
58.q: Well, yeah. Sometime I'd get off step, you know, because I had a way of doing a lot of fingering, you know. And by me doing a lot of fingering, I'd misstep with the, you know, like, with the drum, you know. Boom, boom. It's important to walk right with the drum, you know. But now I'd be playing…

58.t: St. Joseph's Night, the Indians and Mardi Gras bands
58.s: Punch describes Mardi Gras Indians who clashed with each other, the many bands and the parade routes.
58.q: Yeah. Well, yeah, I'll tell you something about that. I never played no dance. I played dance on that, but what I mean, it wasn't just some people in Mass and come to the dance and dance, you know. But I mean, two of them like, be up and down the street, like on Marty Roddy. But did Mass all right,…

58.t: White clubs and burials with music
58.s: Allen asks whether the white carnival clubs buried members with music; Miller says they played carnival and Mardi Gras and would have used white bands.
58.q: Well, if they did, they must have used white bands. They didn't have any color things. Not that I remember.

306.t: Hard parades: the Hobgoblins and the Jackson City Bulls
306.s: Rene recalls playing grueling street parades, including Halloween Hobgoblins and a white club that marched long distances.
306.q: I played so many parades, you know? So many parades, and them parades was hard at them times, you know? Because we used to play the Bulls, they don't have a parade, they're going out existing. The Hobgoblins, you ever heard of them? He used to go on a Halloween night. Well, them fellas used to go…

306.t: Grand marshals and the order of bands and clubs in a parade
306.s: Rene explains the sergeant at arms, first and second grand marshals, and how bands and clubs line up.
306.q: Uh, which one did you call the caller on in the meeting? What they call him? Sergeant of arms? Yeah, that's the one that had the gavel with him. You'll notice him, you see he had the gavel on him. He had the gavel with him in a parade to him.

306.t: How funeral parades began and how Rene started a club
306.s: Rene says the custom started on street corners, and describes forming the White Roses after a man was shot.
306.q: It started with the club. Mostly what I think it started with, from what I can understand, from what I learnt, about 50 or 60 years back, it started from the corners. Like a good fellow was hanging on the corner, you know, and he would die. Well, they would wreck up some money and they would get a…

590.t: Drilling groups, no military service, first dance band
590.s: Alcorn explains the parade drilling groups such as the Odd Fellows, says he was not in the service, and names his first dance band, the Sunny Style Syncopators; the tape runs out.
590.ch: Brass bands and first dance band
590.q: The drilling groups? Well they have little things they do on the street, you know. Quite a while ago they used to have the Tentamere parades around here. And they used to have quite a few drilling groups in there, Odd Fellows and different things. You've never seen the Fancy drill, huh? And they…

590.t: Whether Armstrong played parades and funerals after fame
590.s: Armstrong did not play parades when he came back; Alcorn recalls him as King of the Zulus and giving concerts.
590.ch: Sounds and recording in old New Orleans
590.q: No, he wasn't playing no parades or nothing like that. He never played a parade again? No, he did that. Everybody knew him playing a parade again. No, I mean when he came back.

179.t: Carnival parades and minstrel shows in Algiers
179.s: Carnival parades with school bands; a jazz band was too expensive; no minstrel shows came.
179.q: year yeah yeah they have about three parades over here in carnival did they have the any jazz in the parade or they well they don't have no school band they don't have no regular jazz band they have all them school bands and they don't have no jazz bands only one year about two years back yeah they…

179.s: He goes anywhere music is, followed parades and funerals on foot, and recognizes Dick from parades.
179.q: oh at the clarinet that's merely playing that clarinet oh I thought that was Georgie boy no that's that's mealy no that's just mealy playing that clarinet did you know Georgie boy I heard talk of Georgie boy but I never know him you still like to listen to music well I'll tell you I go anywhere…

250.t: Cack Riley, the lot where parades meet, and his baseball team
250.s: Playing trombone and cornet with Cack, the nearby lot used for Mardi Gras parades, and the ball team he organized, the Cheeky Men.
250.q: I used to play with Cack once in a while, go home and get the cornet, when this boy used to have Lion of Laurel, it used to be George Stokes, they'd put a nickel in his lot in the March of the Bobcats. Cack would get his trombone, walked around, I'd go and get the trombone, they'd have a few beers…

250.t: Scrapbook: benefit game and Mardi Gras bands
250.s: A 1949 benefit game with Tom Brown and Harry Shields, and Bergen on market Mardi Gras bands.
250.q: Every market used to have a band and a little amateur show, Mardi Gras Band. In the old days, it's all been stopped then.

252.t: Spanish-American War veterans' May celebration at Chalmette
252.s: Diggs describes the yearly late-May celebration the veterans attended at Chalmette.
252.q: Well, I'm going to sit out there. You want to get outside, mister? No, no. I was just telling her that she know what I was speaking about. Oh, I see. I'm looking for a letter for my son.

252.t: Benevolent societies and brass bands in Mobile parades
252.s: Diggs says Mobile had the same societies and Spanish-American War ceremonies, with brass bands playing a sad march at opening and closing.
252.q: Yes. The brass bands in our parade. Let me see. Yeah, we had the same way, of course. We had the Spanish-American War and the grand armor celebrated to have a ceremony, the last of May, like that we did here. You understand? Well, I belonged to it and my mother did too. My mother belonged to it…

624.t: Carnival balls and parades, covering two bands with one trumpet
624.s: Brunies played society balls and the five carnival parades; with mule-drawn floats moving slowly, he started one band, ran to start the next and alternated. The music was marches and ragtime marches.
624.ch: Fisher's band and Jack Laine's bands
624.q: We used to play at the Outfellas Hall, big balls like the Druids, Masons and all like that, the Fishies Band, you know. Did they play parades too, like carnival? Parades, yeah. Like carnival parades, we used to have five, uh, five, uh, the whole five carnival parades. The other time I was one…

624.t: Pay for parades and the big carnival clubs
624.s: Pay was low, a dollar and a half or five dollars a night. Brunies and Allen name the main carnival organizations: Rex, Comus, Momus and Proteus.
624.ch: Fisher's band and Jack Laine's bands
624.q: How could a parade pay? Parade, parade, five thousand, man. The big carnival parades, too. Yeah. You mentioned about the five organizations, which were those, Rex and Momus and... All of them, the whole five of them were played.

150.t: Mardi Gras and the Irish Channel street gang
150.s: He recalls watching parades, masking, and fighting in a neighborhood gang with Jonas Monroe, plus the mostly white bands he heard at Carnival.
150.ch: Irish Channel youth, newspapers and McDonogh 35
150.q: Well, when I was a kid, I would cross. My daddy would bring me to the parades when I was, you know, five, six, seven years of age. But as we moved on this side of the river when my mother and father separated, I started leaving 515 Third Street and walking down Jackson Avenue all the way to St.…

150.t: Taft reception brochure and the Jonestown Wolves Club
150.s: He shows a brochure from his grandfather Lewis Taylor's files about the Taft reception, and begins describing Jonestown's marching Wolves Club.
150.q: For William Taff, when you came to the president. President William Howard Taff. You said your grandfather was involved. Yeah, my grandfather was involved with that. What was his name? His name was Taylor, Lewis Taylor. He's not in here. I was looking for him, but this came out of his files. I got…

625.t: St. John Grand Lodge parade and Masonic membership
625.s: Trotter describes playing the 1965 St. John Grand Lodge parade with his Masonic lodge and says he belongs only to that lodge.
625.q: You was out there too. You remember when we played, our Grand Lodge met here, St. John Grand Lodge. See, I'm of that jurisdiction. And I happened to be in one of the bands. That's the Masons. The Masons, that's right.

625.t: Parades: first parade in 1964, older men took them earlier
625.s: Trotter did not play parades in the old days; older musicians took them, and his first was July 1964.
625.q: That group, I don't know, it seemed as though the fellas that were older than what we were, they were taking over the parades, they wouldn't hire us. Mm-hmm. You know, we wouldn't have a chance at the parades. That's the way it was then, you know. Yeah.

251.t: Carnival in Galveston and in New Orleans
251.s: Galveston's Carnival attempt, old neighbourhood masking, social clubs and dances during the season.
251.q: There was something similar to what we do here, but not on a big scale in Galveston years ago. They had tried it. Well, there was a lot of Louisiana people that migrated into Galveston through Beaumont, Texas, and they tried to do the things there that was done in New Orleans, but the people in…

251.t: Street parades, rival bands and police politics
251.s: Albert recalls bands of Sam Morgan and Chris Kelly on parade wagons, bands stopping at corners, and police politics.
251.ch: Parades, vice and the New Orleans scene
251.q: I sat on the ground and sometimes the bands not playing, like with Kidman, Sam Morgan, Chris Kelly. I sat on the ground and even the truck was riding with these guys.

266.t: Lockport Carnival and Mardi Gras versus Philadelphia's Mummers
266.s: They recall Lockport's Carnival on the Saturday before Mardi Gras, then Jones says Philadelphia had no Mardi Gras and the Mummers parade took its place.
266.q: Because most of the people from Lockport would come to New Orleans for Mardi Gras day anyways. Well that makes sense. But it was a while. In fact right after that they started holding it on Fat Tuesday.

266.t: Carnival parades and funeral bands near his father's business
266.s: Jones lived in Lakeview, heard mostly funeral bands near his father's business on Cleveland Avenue, and watched carnival parades near Canal and La Salle.
266.q: No, I lived out in Lakeview. And I never heard too many of those marching bands. In fact, like I said, the only ones that I can remember hearing would be the funeral bands that passed around Cleveland Avenue where my father had his business in that neighborhood. You know, it was black around and…

571.t: Creole carnival songs and Tati's Mardi Gras maskers
571.s: Talk of 'El Abba' and carnival songs leads Alice to her cousin Tati and his lively Mardi Gras group dressed as women.
571.q: Well, he was one of them. He had been, about six or sometimes 12 of them. And they would go around, they dressed in women, and they'd sing, and they'd sing.

571.t: Parade days, Joe Watson and Al Landry's E-flat clarinet
571.s: He describes all-day May parades, fairground bands, and how Al Landry of the Eureka band brought him an E-flat clarinet.
571.q: I mean, you were just talking about the... We played a parade there. Our fellas used to parade from eight in the morning till six in the evening. Uh-huh. All day parade there. Amazons come from, uh... Out the country and everywhere. It was big, big to do over the 30th of May. Me. Uh... They'd have…

269.t: Mardi Gras song 'Fum, fum' and its translation
269.s: She sings a Mardi Gras song Tati used to sing and translates it as a woman being told to sweep the house.
269.q: Mardi Gras songs. Well, uh, let's see if I can remember that song Tati used to sing. Fum, fum, quitte mo balikala, a je fum abadra, that's no good for nothing. Fum, fum, quitte mo balikala, a je fum abadra, tu barrasé moi. Fum, fum, quitte mo balikala, a je fum abadra, tu barrasé moi. Well, that's…

269.t: Creole dancing, costumes and real Indians of her youth
269.s: She describes Creole dances and Indian dress, and real Indians who stayed at her grandmother's and sold at the Indian market.
269.q: Oh, they'd sing all them songs that you're asking me about. They'd sing, they'd dance, the dance of the, you know, Creole dance. And they'd skip. And they'd dress like, well, if there was a bunch of Indians, well, then they would dress like Indians. Now they don't dress like Indians. They would…

601.t: Sunday parades in Algiers and the first parade Martin saw
601.s: Russell asks about parades on the Algiers side. Martin says they were usually held on Sundays, remembers the first parade at Teche and Newton, and lists clubs such as Eagle Eye and the Odd Fellows.
601.q: That's right. They have them on Sundays. The first parade I seen was the last small boy and left... Tash and Newton there. The parade? Yeah. Well, they usually have parades every Sunday. I'm talking about the first parade I seen Tash and Newton. Where, in IJ? Yeah. Well, I never remember no parade…

601.t: Odd Fellows and Masons drilling ranks
601.s: Martin and Tom talk about the Odd Fellows parade and its drilling rank, led by Sam Nanny and George DeVoe, with Shepard Smith as head drillman, and the women's drill team of Miss Patterson that Tom played for.
601.q: No, no, the mason parade over there. They had them on the other side too. Alright, now you take the odd fella parade over there, you take your best drilling rank. Old man Sam Nanny. No, that's right. Yeah, old man Sam Nanny, well he's in the drilling rank. Now you take... Oh, what he... Man, he was…

865.t: Eureka band record, upcoming parades and union cards
865.s: He complains of a poor cymbal on a Eureka record, lists coming parades including Memorial Day at Chalmette, and discusses Casimir and Knox and union cards.
865.q: You know, somebody's been complaining about the simulac. on the Eureka band made a record and that old simulac there is about a $2 simul. It's not a ton. It couldn't be worth more than $2. No tone. It sounds like a... It doesn't sound as good as a tin lid. It sounds like a graveyard symbol. Yeah,…

865.t: Little Jim's parade playing and returning to parades after hospital
865.s: Remarks on a big-drum player, then his doctor lets him march again with the bass drum after illness.
865.ch: Music as a way of life
865.q: He had to look as he was behind the bass. And he played them parades too. Oh yeah, Jim played a many parades. He's in the Cross the River.

706.t: New Orleans funeral marches, brass bands and the first-chair trumpet
706.s: Asked about European composers using jazz, Armstrong describes expressing yourself in funeral marches and the Star-Spangled Banner, and why the lead trumpet matters.
706.q: I play all kind of music when we started out in the dress band in New Orleans playing funeral marches you have to express yourself to play funeral marches the way to play them in New Orleans and it's me as a boy in the mom did never say the difference now up north that come up and they're played a…

706.t: The second line and funeral parade customs
706.s: Armstrong explains the second line in parades, pool hall followers and the grand marshal, and is asked about bands meeting in the street.
706.ch: Joe Oliver and the second line
706.q: What's that? The guys who like to do art fellas, they got on uniforms. Yeah. And they're to parade. Well, you know there's like the pool hall gang. Oh, the guys that, uh, who could drive a car for any chance, but he's got time to follow the parade. Well, they can't get in the parade. So they'd be…

828.t: Peter Claver council, uniforms and Chaligny's band
828.s: The photo was taken near the parish prison; the band belonged to Knights of Peter Claver at St. Catherine's; Humphrey doubted the band was ready for the street.
828.q: Yeah. You can tell them the pillars. Yeah, I never saw, I saw the building years ago, but 15 years, almost 20 years ago.

828.s: The band played at initiations; the picture may date from the day he was initiated in June 1922.
828.q: Oh, yeah. Every time they had initiation there, that's what that was. Initiation there. Yeah, there I am. See? But I'm not...

189.t: Mardi Gras truck jobs and getting lost in the Rex parade
189.s: Pleasure clubs hire bands on trucks; he and Son Johnson get drunk and march off the Rex route.
189.q: You know one time I played a carnival parade, and we were supposed to follow Rex. Yeah. And the guy, the president of the club, it was a white club too, and they gave us a fifth of whiskey. So I was standing next, I was marching with a guy named Son Johnson, have you heard of Son Johnson? Yeah. He…

189.t: Mardi Gras as a child and the Indian tribes
189.s: Watching Zulu and Rex, fear of Indian tribes fighting, tribe names, and his mother's strictness.
189.q: Yes and no. Well, before I would, before I started playing in the parades, and playing on the trucks, we'd stay in front of our house, either go to a jack, two blocks away from our home, where they had the funeral home. That's where the King Zulu used to go and drink his toast. Well, we would go…

121.s: He recalls the Carnival on Claiborne and the streets around it and wishes it had been filmed.
121.q: Oh yeah, well, what I was talking about, the Black Carnival downtown on Arlene Street. You see, I mean, from Arlene and Claiborne on down to Arlene and St. Bernard, this was a Carnival, and then on Melford, I never did go on Melford Mean Street from, well, it's Martin Luther King now, from…

121.t: Brass bands and playing on a parade truck in 1957
121.s: A band truck out of the Ninth Ward with Justin Adams on amplified guitar, white clubs he played for, and a brass band he cannot name.
121.q: little marching club with a brass band. And I'm talking about blacks. There was always a band coming along the street, somebody playing, you really don't know who they are. But there's always a, you would always hear marching band. Now, Herman Sherman, you remember Herman Sherman? No, he died. He…

819.t: Carnival parades then and now, pay for parades
819.s: They lament today's carnival parades and recall playing five parades for $15, routes and the old hired bands.
819.q: That's what I'm missing. In this carnival praise, that's why I think it's actually disgraceful. I mean, we used to have some good bands out there. Yeah, that's really, I heard something. What I heard in that parade, brother. The people used to go wild. The band used to take them off their feet.…

819.t: Tunes played in parades and the lost Millenburg picnics
819.s: Parade repertoire (Tiger Rag, marches), the atmosphere of old parades, and the end of picnics at Millenburg.
819.q: I heard a band in the parade here. Union band. I think it was absolutely. It was absolutely off. I don't know what it was. Because the rest of them were all kid bands, you know. School bands.

648.t: First brass band job for a carnival club

875.q: Yeah, I worked with Abby a lot. Worked with Abby a lot, little jobs. Where? Well down around Paul Good and Burgundy, and Paul Good around the corner in 59. When I first began to get into the air like that, I was working with him down there then.

800.t: Mardi Gras work with Harry Robichaud
800.s: Talk of Harry Robichaud, and Alexander says he has played with him on Mardi Gras day for seven years, for carnival club dances.
800.q: Yeah, I've been playing with him on that day, you know, for the last seven years.

188.s: He led a brass band with violin in carnival parades, played advertising wagons, and enjoyed band contests; Big Eye Louis called him a jazz fiddler.
188.q: Out on the street? Out on the street, I had my, they hired my band. That's all there's an issue with them. Well, I had to hire three more to make ten pieces, you know. And you took your violin out. I did some walking that carnival. For the Jefferson City budget. You know where they are up there on…

675.t: Brass band tempos and the best bands from LaPlace
675.s: Braud explains brass bands used six-eighth and two-four time on the street, and praises the Dejan and Claiborne Williams brass bands, who read and improvised.
675.q: They have what they call six-eighth time. They have what they call to play some in two full time. See what I mean? Well, who would use those? Well, brass bands, like a minister band, they use six-eighth time for the street. You understand? And some tunes, they used two full times. And some tunes,…

190.t: Parade work: marching with Paul Barbarin
190.s: Purnell says he played only two days of parades, with Paul Barbarin's band, including Labor Day on Canal Street, and wanted no more.
190.q: Well, see, I was in the man so much around that, see, when you come to the parade, I played a parade. I played a parade. I played a walk in high. Once I played a parade. Twice, two days, I played. I played with Paul Barbarin. Boy, and then people walking from nine o'clock that morning to six…

182.t: Choosing easier tunes late in long parades
182.s: Hard marches were played first and easier pieces when tired on the way back.
182.q: Easy? A little easier? Yes. Sometimes you get tired and you pick up a little anything which you think is easy. Yeah. So there's hard marches where we play them when we first start. Yeah, that's right. Yeah, there's hard marches. You see we play them, sometimes you get some tough pieces of march…

876.t: Boyhood parades and playing alto in brass bands
876.s: He loved following parades as a boy and later played alto horn in the Tulane band and with old man Henry Allen's funerals and parades.
876.q: Oh, well, I used to run all the parades, and all the advertisement on the... I was a band that was playing on the corner. I'd be out there. And the parades, and my mother never allowed me to follow the parades. But if they came around the neighborhood I'd follow them a block or two anyway. I used…

283.t: Johnny Lala and the 50-piece Italian parade band
283.s: Talk of Johnny Lala, who played Schilling's band and stayed home rather than go to New York, and of the Italian band in uniform playing parades.
283.q: Well, he was... The guy was supposed to go with what's called Dixieland Band, to New York, see. But he wouldn't go because he had a meat market with his dad. And so he says, no, I can make more money here. But he was a better trumpet player than Nick, you know. I mean, he moved the band. That's…

877.t: Carnival parades and flutes in Pass Christian
877.s: Pass Christian had Mardi Gras floats and parades; Handy and his father and brothers played up and down the streets, and the father bought the boys instruments.
877.q: Well, well, well, well, we had, we had, uh, one of the best, uh, parades. It was, I imagine, during the time that we had parades here, we had them in Pastor Christian. And we had some very, very wonderful flutes. Is that at Mardi Gras time? Mardi Gras times. Albert Alexander had flutes. He sat down…

841.t: Brass bands, funerals and Labor Day parades
841.s: Harris played funerals and parades with Allen, Williams, the Eureka and Tuxedo bands before he was crippled.
841.q: Yeah, I used to play with old man Rowley, I mean, uh, Allen. Oh, man. Old man. I used to play with him. I'd play a funeral with George Williams. I'd play a funeral with, um, I don't know, before I got crippled, I used to play all the funerals and parades. And don't talk about Labor Day. You know,…

878.t: Street parade bands and their ragtime repertoire
878.s: Harry describes ten-piece street bands playing Mardi Gras parades without written music: popular tunes like Pretty Baby, Tiger Rag and High Society.
878.q: Oh, I'd say, well, sometimes two trumpets, uh, two cornets rather, and two trombones, tuba, and they'd have a baritone, upright out, clarinet, two drums. Yeah.

288.t: The Swells club parades and the unruly second line
288.s: He recalls all-day parades for the Swells with second liners who danced and misbehaved.
288.q: But I'm going to tell you all one thing. I've always asked the Almighty God. Because those fellows like Manetta and Phil and Boca and them, they used to tell me these things and I used to deny them. You see? In other words I was wondering that I'm doubting Thomas.

8.s: A big carnival-like holiday with parades and lodge bands from other cities.
8.q: That was a big time. It was like something like carnival, you know, in that old school. Big parade. Different lodges coming from different... cities, you know.

879.s: The band's city hall Flag Day parade and a substitute who filled in.
879.q: Uh, well that particular day, Kimball, uh, he didn't perform that day. Uh-huh. Uh. You have a duo player? Well no, but that particular day too, uh, we, uh, Jared Green came along and played with us, uh, he dedicated his service to the post office.

635.t: Mardi Gras and Sunday wagon bands
635.s: Bands rode furniture wagons through the city on Mardi Gras, getting food and drink at houses and saloons.
635.q: I would be playing on one of those wagons, see? You'd be at the wagons. Oh I see. Like a bunch of you guys, like you say, you got about eight guys that are ready to get a big furniture wagon. Put your little band, get your three or six piece band in, wagon, build a wagon. The guy would be hanging…

726.t: Two-fold marches and dropping down to the chorus
726.s: Cie asks how two-fold marches go. Williams plays snare and bass drum on a march (Maryland suggested), counts it and drops down to the chorus, then asks how to end it. Much of the text is garbled.
726.q: Oh, the two-fold, well, you have to beat on the snare, you see, you hit the bass drum. What's the two-fold mark I can think about? Let's see. I'm trying to think of most now with a two-fold.

193.t: Brass bands, funerals and Mardi Gras
193.s: He lists brass bands he worked with, including DeJalma Gagne's, for funerals and Mardi Gras.
193.q: Yeah, I worked with Gagne. How often did you play with him? Well, whenever we'd get a funeral parade, they'd get them quite often.

880.t: When the Holmes photo was taken and the band's city visits
880.s: Joseph dates the picture about 1901; the band came to New Orleans for carnival, playing parades and dances.
880.q: numbers where they'd get off a lot? Oh yeah sure they could. They came down here and cleaned up all the band in the street band in the city. Uh huh. Carnival you know. Used to come down here. Carnival. Yeah.

194.t: Mardi Gras Indians rehearsing at his house
194.s: He rehearsed alongside the Wild Magnolias and Wild Tchoupitoulas; SPEAKER_03 explains the tribes' split.
194.q: Well, I know, uh, Wild Chapitulas, and, uh, Wild Magnolias, and really, we all have rehearsals together. I mean, the Wild Magnolias, we've rehearsed in the same building, from 70 up until about 73, the Indian tribes.

881.t: The second line, rough New Orleans wards, and his mother's support
881.s: He describes following second-line parades, dangerous wards, the Didn't He Ramble tune, whistling for Oliver, and his debt to his mother.
881.ch: New Orleans second line and Armstrong
881.q: Yeah, well the second line, the second line. I guess I just always was crazy about music. Doing that whistling and going on I did. I guess it just was destined for me to be a musician. I believe in predestination. I believe when a person is first born, that is like a big book, there's so much he's…

855.t: Brass band parade in Berlin with Keith Smith's band
855.s: In 1963 Berlin friends and the English band organized a street parade; police stopped it for lack of permission.
855.ch: Reception in Germany and Berlin scene
855.q: Key Smith's Climax Band, 1963, the first time in Berlin the whole band had lived at home we were very good friends and we had then for Sunday, for the Sunday, when the band didn't play, no it was the afternoon, we had to talk about a brass band to form so we knew from the albums and the English had…

22.t: La Rocca on Kepard, Oliver, carnival parades and funeral bands
22.s: La Rocca says Black bands never played carnival parades, older players had to copy the ODJB rhythm, and funeral marches were not jazz.
22.ch: La Rocca on who created jazz
22.q: Now, they say that this, but Freddie Kepit, they make a great big story about it, that he was asked by the Victor Company to record. He says he didn't want to record because he didn't want the world to know his stuff. But they didn't know that I knew all this stuff. They thought that I was just a…

689.t: The planned street brass band stopped by the union
689.s: Dominique says a brass band with Oliver, Armstrong and Lee Collins was planned, but the union stopped it.
689.q: A street band. And we had the band to do it. George Field, the Dutre. And that fellow, what's his name to get a trombone player? Oh, I know him. Kid O'Ree. And they had, oh, we had about two of us. Oh, I know him. Oh, well, he died. Well, they didn't let us put up that brass band of Louis, myself,…

882.t: Jake Steves and the Maccabees band, and Picou
882.s: Jake Steves's white Maccabees band, which gave him the carnival parade work, and Picou playing with him.
882.q: Steve. And the name of the band was the Maccabees band. Maccabees. I don't know of any of his people. That was a white band. Yes. Yes.

883.t: Music in New Iberia: Banner Band and absence of parades
883.s: She recalls hearing the Banner Band and old standards, and says New Iberia had no parades or brass bands until the later Sugar Festival.
883.q: Well, I used to go to Jules Bob Band, used to have a band. They used to come to New Iberia. And of course the Banner Band used to have all the music, because they were most of the standard bands. They'd been there when you were a girl too.

830.t: Where George played: country clubs, halfway house, carnival parades
830.s: He played country clubs, the Halfway House, dances at West End and carnival parades for the Jefferson City Buzzards; cornet was his only instrument.
830.q: They played all, but he mostly played for the country club. And he used to play, what, the halfway house. What was that? He played out the halfway house. He played day every night most. Halfway house for a long time.

884.t: Mardi Gras and parades on the Algiers side
884.s: People from New Orleans came to Algiers at Mardi Gras; a white club had a parade and hired his three-piece field band.
884.ch: Algiers parades and the wider city
884.q: Oh, gee, we used to take people coming from New Orleans over here.

690.t: Mardi Gras king's arrival and bugle calls
690.s: Pope's father played flourishes and bugle calls when the king and queen came in on Mardi Gras.
690.q: I don't recall just the right tiles for them, you know. But it's something you made up? They would come in, you know. They would call the bugle calls, and bury me, you know. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Like that. That's it. I just wish I had a little time, you understand? Well, that's all right.

885.t: Mardi Gras as a child and the Indians
885.s: Watching Rex, Zulu and the Mardi Gras Indians pass in his neighborhood and masking as a clown.
885.q: Yeah, well for me as a kid it was a great day because we used to go to, my daddy used to bring me to the old bayou just before you get to the train station that used to be. I forgot what it was, I was a child. That's where the floats used to come out on Galleup Street and they used to come through…

192.t: Early street parades with the Tuxedo Brass Band
192.s: Frazier talks about funeral marches and being started on parades by Trepagnier in the original Tuxedo Brass Band.
192.q: It's mostly the same stuff you play in the day. Lots of funeral marches. I'll tell you how the bands did them days. Any band had a funeral march. They'd take the name of it, so the other band wouldn't know the name of it. Yeah, yeah. And the first man that started me on the parade was Ones…

886.t: Second line fights and the Jolly Bunch
886.s: Second line fights with bricks and knives have calmed down; the Jolly Bunch is the best club now.
886.q: Oh, right. They fight like they don't. They use knives and stuff. Sometimes they're not cutting and shooting too. Yeah. Big old drum hammer. Beat you over.

293.t: Jelly Roll at the Orleans Pleasure Club
293.s: Jelly Roll Morton came to the club around 1920 or earlier, brought by Freddie Lucian's father; the club's location and his dislike of parades.
293.ch: Orleans Pleasure Club to PWA band
293.q: Well, them guys used to be around there, you see, and this guy brought him around, this Freddie Lucian brought Jelly Roll more than to our club when we got the piano.

295.t: Mardi Gras parades and playing five or six jobs in one day
295.s: He recalls snow on his first big Mardi Gras parade (1899, per Allen) and one Mardi Gras day of several jobs, from an advertising wagon to the day and night parades and the Merry Whittier ball.
295.q: no, I really couldn't, but I remember though... Approximately. I remember one time, that, it started to snow on the Mardi Gras day. That was the first big Mardi Gras parade ever I made. It started to snow one time, but I don't remember just now, the year that was in. But that's been, oh, good…

573.t: Playing in parades with Sam and Chris Kelly
573.s: He played only two parades, hating walking and playing, one with Sam and Chris Kelly.
573.ch: Playing New Orleans and the coast
573.q: Who me? I haven't played, well, yes, I played two parades in New Orleans since I've been a musician. I played on Labor Day. I played with Sam and Chris Kelly. They was playing a brass band. Playing a parade. And they fooled me. And I didn't want to go and play. And they asked me to play. And I…

296.t: Firemen's Day parades, carnival and Bastille Day
296.s: Playing the firemen's anniversary parade and banquet; no parades but picnics on July 14.
296.q: For the March. For the March. For the March. For the March, that was the anniversary. Oh, yeah. Ask him what they did.

782.t: Parades, shootings and the repertoire of second-line bands
782.s: He criticizes violence at parades and the constant repetition of blues, wishing for real marches.
782.ch: Brass bands, funerals and Swedish scene
782.q: It was about the same. The week before the Jolly Bunch, I think it was the week before, maybe it was the Jolly Bunch, there was some shooting, some guns.

837.t: Mardi Gras parades passing his house
837.s: As a child of six or seven he saw Mardi Gras parades with one jazz band, Jack Laine's, stopping before his house. People danced in the street and the militia met the king.
837.q: There was, but there were not as many as there were today. And there was none of these formations of marching high school girls and boys. The only time they used what they called the militia then was on the day before Mardi Gras, which has been dispensed with.

735.t: Parades and funerals with Kid Rena; watching the Tuxedo band
735.s: How seldom Rena's band got parades, the clubs that hired them, how parades looked, and how few funerals they played.
735.q: Well that was seldom. They didn't have as many parades as they have now. And just whenever Renee would get a parade well he'd use me to play with him. And that wouldn't be too often. That'd be some Sundays. Like different clubs would have a turn out. Well they'd use his band and I'd get a chance to…

666.t: Fraternity parties, Earl Crum and his mother's house
666.s: The band played fraternity parties and balls as carnival revived after the war, through promoter and drummer Earl Crum, whose mother's house on Lee Circle they used for practice.
666.q: Yeah. It was Monk played the guitar. I remember he had a hell of a fine guitar. Somebody had bought over in Italy and brought to this country. I think it was Bill Kleppinger. He was one of his good friends. I think Bill lived at his house. He was living on Napoleon and Ronaldette I believe it was.…

766.s: He played parades only once or twice and disliked the walking; one was with Thomas Copeland for the carnival.
766.q: What you call him playing bass drum? What you call him? Parker, remember that? Big tall Parker. Parker. He died then. That was a good bass. He died then. Tom Parker. Tom Parker, yeah. That was a good one. I don't know.

858.t: Tulane brass band and why he stopped playing brass bands
858.s: He played in the Tulane brass band with Landry and Rodgers on drums, sometimes two parades a day, and no longer does.
858.ch: Brass bands and the WPA band
858.q: Mm-hm. Who had such men as Dalkywall Warner and Dalkywall. and Landry, a few of them, I can't think of just young. Some of them were practically old, nearly all of them were dead. Rodgers was playing drums.

832.t: Picnics and parades in Mandeville; Bunk Johnson
832.s: Foster recalls New Orleans bands at picnics, parades by the Independent Band, bands riding in open trucks, and Bunk Johnson, who gave him his nickname Brother.
832.q: Well, that was during, I think, the 7th at a time then. Even that then? Yeah, that was during, well that was, that was in the 20th then. That was in the 20th. Yeah, that was during the 20th when the band was for one of the big pieces. I know, bands from New Orleans, yeah.

574.t: Eureka Brass Band, parades and carnival at Thibodaux
574.s: The local Eureka Brass Band, its size, occasional parades by societies, and the Thibodaux carnival.
574.q: Sometimes they have a parade, uh, like the old fellas turn out like that, well, they have a little parade. For the different organizations then? Yeah. See, and them times, uh, they used to play for that carnival in Tebido.

303.t: First Famous Door band photos; Rex bandwagon aside
303.s: Photos of Sharkey's first band at the Famous Door, with Santo, Lester and Chink Martin, and the Coca Room at the auditorium. Allen asks about playing for costumed Mardi Gras balls; Riddick says he played on the Rex bandwagon four straight years.
303.ch: Scrapbook: Sharkey Bonano years at the Famous Door
303.q: Yeah. Once in a while. He never had a tuba of his own at that time. Yeah. And someone would loan it to him.

305.s: The big Mardi Gras parade features dozens of Dixieland bands on trucks, many from outside New Orleans.
305.q: any time... No... never... as a matter of fact... on Monte Grande... the largest single parade... uh... in the halls... probably... in the United States... with the... this is some... uh... 190... 200... decorated trucks... and on those trucks... there'll be approximately... 45 or 50 bands...…

308.t: Night parades, the Hop Goblins and other clubs
308.s: Talk of the parade route down Claiborne and the women's Hop Goblins club with flambeau lights and costumes.
308.q: Well, I think they were separate from the Bulls, the Hop Goblins. It was a different organization.

887.t: Carnival, Indians and a parade Cahn attended that day
887.s: Cahn says tribes would not exist without Carnival and describes a large parade of four groups in matching colors that he watched earlier that day.
887.q: I'm not a, I'm not much on popular music, as you would call it, on your rock and so forth. Yeah. I've tried to tune it out.

309.t: Mardi Gras and balls on the Gulf Coast
309.s: He describes small Mardi Gras floats and parades, fish sandwiches on excursion trains, and playing for schools and balls.
309.ch: Hotels, Mardi Gras and the Gulf Coast
309.q: Mardi Gras was one of them. In other words, they had a fellow by the name of Albert Alexander. And he had a little group there and they used to build floats and all like that. And we used to play on the floats just like they did here. But I mean, it was just a smaller group and everything. But…

888.t: Mardi Gras, Tremé and passing on New Orleans culture
888.s: Marching clubs, neighbourhood musicians, tap dancing like the Nicholas Brothers, Tremé and Preservation Hall shaped her sense of heritage.
888.q: Let me answer that this way. I became aware of it because of some things that happened in New Orleans, the Mardi Gras. Okay? My parents were in a marching club. So at Mardi Gras they dressed in these costumes and had the band and they marched around. And I grew up with that. And it was understood…

889.s: Describes the long marching-and-concert feast schedule, which required endurance; a lesson with Armando Ghitalla confirms its value; Rowe wonders about New Orleans parades.
889.q: Yeah. We would start the feast on the day before and we would start at 8 in the morning. Italian bands, however, don’t march in step, they just walk. They don’t march in step, they just walk and play. Because all the marches, the old Italian marches, they’re like little overtures, They’re not like…

813.t: Failed New Orleans parade and wagon bands
813.s: Parade drumming plans with Chris Tyle derailed when the leader played 'The Saints' too fast; Disneyland wagon parades and Kid Ory.
813.q: With the trombone hanging over the back. I’d love to play a job like that. I got a chance to play a parade down there, and for weeks, and this fellow Chris, who is also a fine drummer, we were going to play drums, bass drum and snare drum. We studied Bunk’s Brass Band and the Eureka Brass Band, and…

64.t: Founding Jazzmobile with a parade float in Harlem
64.s: With the Harlem Culture Council he gets a Ballantine float and electric piano to bring live jazz through Harlem, then adds workshops.
64.q: what we should do is have jazz as a first project. And I couldn’t find a way to make them do that. And a woman named Daphne Onstein went out to the World’s Fair and said, you know, with all these millions of dollars of buildings and all these things that people spent money on, here are people…

558.t: Havana carnival comparsas and playing snare for Los Alacranes
558.s: Each neighbourhood had a comparsa; he played snare drum for El Cerro's Los Alacranes, marching two hours to the jury on the Prado, competing in a friendly spirit.
558.q: (Laughs) In fact I was going to tell you about that. Each neighborhood has its comparsa. But not because I'm from El Cerro but in the Traditional category, my neighborhood’s comparsa, Los Alacranes (The Scorpions), always took the first prize in the Traditional category. Now the comparsa in the…

229.t: Marching and concert bands in the sixties
229.s: In the sixties he plays in the Urban Concert Band, the Elks, Shriners and Letter Carriers bands while still working for the school district.
229.ch: Family, marching bands and the tavern
229.q: During the sixties I was playing other types of music besides jazz. I was a member of a number of marching bands, concert bands, even a community symphony orchestra. Most of my work at that time was with the Urban Concert Band.

145.t: The 1939 Labor Day parade and the original Jazzmobile
145.s: Royal, vice president of Local 767, organized trucks with Basie, Lunceford and his band with King Cole's trio, passing Hampton's house.
145.ch: Hite tours, postwar L.A. and the Central Avenue scene
145.q: Oh, he was sort of in with it. So really, what gave him the idea of that was the fact that in the year 1939, Labor Day, they had a great big parade which was always the thing in California of having the Labor Day Parade. On this particular Labor Day, two big bands were in town. It was the Count…

641.t: New Orleans bands in Baton Rouge: Kid Ory battles and Mardi Gras
641.s: Joe recalls only New Orleans bands coming to Baton Rouge, including Kid Ory battling Toots Johnson, and the town's own Mardi Gras.
641.q: I never remembered Evan Thomas or any of those other bands coming into Baton Rouge. The bands I remember mostly were all New Orleans bands, including Kid

18.t: Parades and the Knights of Pythias band
18.s: They played only around the school; later he marched in the KP band down Seventh Avenue without reading music.
18.ch: Family, Margaret's story and Eutris's memories
18.q: I played in that band; I forgot. I sure did, and couldn't read a note. Came all the way from Atlanta to New York and paraded down Seventh Avenue.

29.t: Jimmie Lunceford's band in the Labor Day parade
29.s: Howard recalls Lunceford's band representing Local 767 in a Labor Day parade and the union marching band.
29.ch: Quality Serenaders, Cotton Club and union recollections
29.q: Yes, they did have. Now, I can't remember what that was. You'll have to forgive me. There are some things you can't remember.
